title: write 40 bytes past the end: over the neighbour, into a third live object
object: a, 24 bytes, the first of three consecutive st_alloc(24)
neighbour: under a 16-byte-aligned arena a=[0,32) b=[32,64) c=[64,96), so a[64] is c[0]

asan.why: The row where ANNOTATION FAILS FOR A SPATIAL BUG: a[64] lands on c[0], which is a live object and must stay unpoisoned, so no poison-on-allocate scheme can object. On malloc the verdict depends on ASan's redzone width: offset 64 clears a's right redzone and lands in a later live object, so it is MISSED too (marked to verify; measured MISSED on the lab server and on EC2).

valgrind.why: Pools: the destination byte is c[0], addressable and owned, so MISSED with or without annotation. malloc: Memcheck replaces malloc with its own allocator, which puts a redzone (16 bytes by default) around every block, so a+64 falls between blocks, not in a live one, and is DETECTED (the original prediction, MISSED, was marked to verify and was wrong; measured on the lab server and on EC2).

hwasan.why: a[64] lands in the third object. On malloc, and in the pool once the allocator tags objects, that object carries a different tag, so the check fires wherever the overflow lands -- which poisoning cannot do once it lands in a LIVE object (ASan's annotated columns are MISSED). Unannotated, all three objects share the pool's tag.

ubsan.why: -fsanitize=bounds needs a statically known array bound; a pointer out of an allocator has none. The row is kept so the report can say UBSan is not a heap tool rather than leaving it out.

lowfat.why: Offset 64 leaves the 32-byte size class, so LowFat reports on malloc -- the opposite of cases 1 and 2. Under an arena the bounds are the pool's and nothing leaves it.

status: written; formal runs 2026-11-13: ASan and Valgrind on the lab server (x86-64), HWASan in the aarch64 Lima VM
